questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 4 day history of blurred vision in her left eye. She sees brief flashes of light when she moves the eye, and the eye aches, especially on looking to the side. Colours look dull in that eye. Visual acuity is 6/18 left and 6/6 right. The eye is white and dilated fundoscopy shows a flat retina and normal disc.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Subacute monocular blurring with pain on eye movement and colour desaturation is optic neuritis; photopsia can occur. A flat retina excludes detachment.

clues: brief flashes of light when she moves the eye
steps.x: Young woman, **subacute**, **pain on movement**, **colour loss**. Flashes are a recognised feature; the retina is flat.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Optic neuritis.

elim: Gives a red, painful eye with halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
Gives a red eye with photophobia.
Floaters and flashes without colour loss or pain on movement.
Gives flashes and a curtain, but the retina is flat and painless.

steps.x: **C. Optic neuritis.** Photopsia can occur in optic neuritis; check the retina to exclude detachment.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has lost vision in both eyes over 2 days, with eye pain. A week later she develops weakness in both legs and urinary retention. Acuity is counting fingers in both eyes. MRI spine shows a cord lesion extending over 7 vertebral segments. MRI brain shows no typical MS lesions.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her optic neuritis?
questions.e: Bilateral, rapid, severe optic neuritis with a longitudinally extensive cord lesion and bladder dysfunction is neuromyelitis optica (anti-aquaporin-4).

steps.x: **Bilateral**, **fast**, plus **longitudinally extensive** myelitis and bladder involvement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neuromyelitis optica.

elim: Affects over-50s with headache and jaw claudication, not myelitis.
Usually unilateral optic neuritis and short cord lesions.
Possible but less likely without systemic features; the long cord lesion fits NMO.
Painless, symmetrical and slow, without a long inflammatory cord lesion.

steps.x: **C. Neuromyelitis optica.** NMO: bilateral ON, long cord lesions, AQP4 antibodies.

questions.stem: An ophthalmology registrar is teaching about two patients with acute unilateral visual loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect. One is a 29 year old woman whose vision worsened over 5 days. The other is a 74 year old man whose vision was lost overnight, with a new headache and scalp tenderness.
questions.q: Which feature most strongly favours optic neuritis over ischaemic optic neuropathy?
questions.e: Optic neuritis gives pain on eye movement and a subacute course; ischaemic optic neuropathy (e.g. GCA) gives headache and a more acute onset.

clues: lost overnight, with a new headache
steps.x: Optic neuritis: **pain on movement**, subacute. Ischaemic: **headache**, sudden.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pain on eye movement.

elim: Favours giant cell arteritis and ischaemic optic neuropathy.
Ischaemic loss is more acute; optic neuritis is subacute.

steps.x: **C. Pain on eye movement.** ON hurts on movement; AION hurts the head.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis for 2 months. He now notices that reds and greens look washed out and reading is harder in both eyes. His acuity is 6/12 in each eye. Fundoscopy is normal. He takes four drugs for TB.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis with reduced acuity and red-green colour loss, so patients need visual acuity and colour vision monitoring.

clues: treated for pulmonary tuberculosis for 2 months
reds and greens look washed out
steps.x: TB drug + **colour vision loss** = **ethambutol**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ethambutol.

elim: Given to prevent isoniazid neuropathy; does not harm the optic nerve.
Causes orange secretions, hepatitis and enzyme induction.

steps.x: **A. Ethambutol.** Ethambutol: monitor acuity and colour vision.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman had right optic neuritis 2 years ago, treated with steroids. Her right acuity recovered to 6/6. At a routine review she says colours still look slightly duller in her right eye. There is a mild right RAPD. She has had no new symptoms. Her MRI brain was normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her ongoing symptom?
o: Persistent colour vision impairment after optic neuritis
questions.e: Even after acuity recovers, a persistent visual deficit, especially colour vision impairment and a mild RAPD, often remains.

steps.x: Recovered acuity, **stable** mild colour loss after optic neuritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A persistent deficit after optic neuritis.

elim: Would blur acuity and develop over years of steroid use.
Would be progressive, and her symptom has been stable.
Gives peripheral field loss with cupping.
Gives sudden curtain loss, not stable colour change.

steps.x: **C. Persistent colour vision impairment after optic neuritis.** Long term: persistent deficit, recurrence, colour impairment.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has her first episode of left optic neuritis. She asks what it means for her future health. She has no other neurological symptoms. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. MRI is pending.
questions.q: Approximately what proportion of patients with optic neuritis develop or already have multiple sclerosis?
questions.e: Between 40 and 70% of patients with optic neuritis develop or have MS, the biggest long-term association.

clues: first episode of left optic neuritis
steps.x: MS is the commonest cause and the **biggest long-term association**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Far too low; MS is the biggest long-term association.
Too high; many never develop MS.

steps.x: **B. 40 to 70%.** 40 to 70% develop or have MS.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has reduced vision in his left eye only. Covering the left eye, his vision is normal; covering the right eye, everything is blurred. He has a central scotoma in the left eye and the right field is full. Eye movements are painful on the left.
questions.q: Where is the lesion most likely to be?
questions.e: A lesion of one optic nerve causes visual loss in the same eye only. Lesions at or behind the chiasm affect both eyes' fields.

clues: reduced vision in his left eye only
steps.x: **Monocular** loss = the lesion is in front of the chiasm, on the **same side**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Left optic nerve.

elim: Gives a right homonymous hemianopia affecting both eyes.

steps.x: **B. Left optic nerve.** Ipsilateral optic nerve lesion = ipsilateral visual loss.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 3 day history of painful blurred vision in her right eye with red desaturation and a right RAPD. Fundoscopy of the right eye shows a swollen, hyperaemic optic disc. The left disc is normal. She has no headache, and her BP is 118/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate description of the right fundoscopic finding?
o: Optic disc swelling from optic neuritis
questions.e: Fundoscopy is often normal early but can show acute disc swelling; papilloedema is reserved for swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure.

steps.x: Unilateral swollen disc with normal BP and no headache: **not** papilloedema.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Disc swelling due to optic neuritis.

elim: A pale disc seen chronically, not acutely.
Means disc swelling from raised ICP, usually bilateral with headache.

steps.x: **D. Optic disc swelling from optic neuritis.** Papilloedema = disc swelling from raised ICP only.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 1 week history of an ache behind her right eye on eye movement and slightly blurred vision. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes and confrontation fields are full. Fundoscopy is normal in both eyes. The doctor wants an objective sign of optic nerve dysfunction.
questions.q: Which examination finding is most likely?
o: Right ptosis with a dilated pupil
Right red eye with ciliary injection
questions.e: A RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil) is the signature sign: on the swinging light test the affected pupil appears to dilate, and it can be present even with normal acuity.

clues: ache behind her right eye on eye movement
steps.x: Normal acuity and discs, but symptoms in the right eye: look for an **afferent** defect.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Right RAPD.

elim: Raised ICP; her discs are normal.
The symptoms are in the right eye.
A third nerve palsy, an efferent problem.

steps.x: **E. Right relative afferent pupillary defect.** RAPD can be present even with 6/6 acuity.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has a 6 day history of reduced vision in her left eye. It aches when she looks around. The eye is white and not photophobic, and the pupil reacts. Acuity is 6/24 left. She has a central scotoma and a left RAPD. Fundoscopy is normal. Intraocular pressure is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Subacute painful monocular loss with a central scotoma, RAPD and white eye is optic neuritis; the mimics have been excluded by the examination.

clues: eye is white and not photophobic
central scotoma and a left RAPD
steps.x: Pain on movement + scotoma + RAPD + **white, normal-pressure eye**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Optic neuritis.

elim: Red eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil and high pressure.
Sudden painless loss with a cherry red spot.
Painless curtain with an abnormal retina.

steps.x: **D. Optic neuritis.** Exclude AACG, retinal detachment, uveitis and stroke.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has painful blurred vision in her right eye with a right RAPD. She also has tender red lumps on her shins and a dry cough for 2 months. Chest X-ray (see item resources). Her calcium is 2.74 mmol/L (2.2–2.6). MRI brain shows no white matter lesions.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her optic neuritis?
questions.e: Optic neuritis with erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and hypercalcaemia points to sarcoidosis.

clues: tender red lumps on her shins
steps.x: Erythema nodosum + **BHL** + high calcium = **sarcoid**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sarcoidosis.

elim: No brain lesions, and it does not explain the hilar nodes, erythema nodosum or calcium.
No myelitis, and it does not explain the chest findings.
Does not cause bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
Possible with hilar nodes, but erythema nodosum, high calcium and BHL fit sarcoid.

steps.x: **C. Sarcoidosis.** Causes of ON beyond MS: sarcoid, NMO, ethambutol.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 5 day history of blurred vision in her left eye and pain when looking up. Her acuity is 6/12 in the left eye. She has a left RAPD. She is asked to describe how the world looks through the left eye compared with the right.
questions.q: Which is the most likely description?
questions.e: Reduced colour vision, especially red desaturation, is a hallmark of optic neuritis, shown by reduced Ishihara scores.

clues: blurred vision in her left eye
steps.x: Optic nerve disease: **colour** is lost early, especially **red**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Red desaturation.

elim: Acute angle-closure glaucoma or corneal oedema.

steps.x: **D. Red objects look faded.** Red desaturation = optic nerve.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has a 1 week history of painful loss of vision in his right eye, worse on eye movement. Acuity is 6/36 right, 6/6 left. He has a right RAPD and a central scotoma. The left eye is normal. He eats a normal diet and drinks 6 units a week.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Subacute, painful, unilateral loss with a RAPD is optic neuritis. Compressive lesions are insidious and painless; nutritional causes are bilateral with no RAPD.

steps.x: Subacute, **painful**, **unilateral**, RAPD.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Optic neuritis.

elim: Painless, and usually affects both eyes in sequence.
Bilateral and symmetrical with no RAPD.

steps.x: **D. Optic neuritis.** Compressive = slow and painless; nutritional = bilateral, no RAPD.

questions.stem: A GP is reviewing the histories of five patients who all report recent visual loss in one eye. All are between 25 and 75 years old and none has a red eye. Only one has optic neuritis. Each history describes a different onset and associated feature, and the GP must decide who needs urgent referral.
questions.q: Which history best fits optic neuritis?
o: A curtain coming across the vision over an hour
Loss of vision for 5 minutes then full recovery
Vision worsening over several days with pain on eye movement
questions.e: Optic neuritis is a subacute monocular loss, worsening over days, with pain on eye movement.

clues: recent visual loss in one eye
steps.x: Optic neuritis: **subacute** (days) and **painful on movement**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Days of worsening with pain on movement.
**E. Vision worsening over several days with pain on eye movement.** Subacute and painful = optic neuritis.

questions.stem: A neurologist reviews a 32 year old woman with optic neuritis. Her vision has fallen to 6/36 in the affected eye. She is deciding whether this is typical MS-related optic neuritis or neuromyelitis optica, as the treatment and prognosis differ. The woman's pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which finding would most strongly suggest neuromyelitis optica?
questions.e: NMO gives bilateral, quicker-onset optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive cord lesions, bladder dysfunction, leg weakness and anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies.

clues: deciding whether this is typical MS-related optic neuritis or neuromyelitis optica
steps.x: NMO = **long** cord lesions, bilateral ON, AQP4.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Longitudinally extensive cord lesion.

elim: Typical MS pattern; NMO is often bilateral.

steps.x: **A. Longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion.** NMO: long cord lesions; MS: short lesions, periventricular plaques.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman has right optic neuritis. MRI of the brain, orbits and whole spine with contrast has been performed. The neurologist explains that one finding would mean she is at much higher risk of multiple sclerosis. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which MRI finding is she referring to?
questions.e: MRI looks for demyelinating plaques suggestive of MS; periventricular white matter lesions mean a high risk of MS.

clues: much higher risk of multiple sclerosis
steps.x: MRI is done to look for **demyelinating plaques**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Periventricular white matter lesions.

elim: Suggests a pituitary adenoma, unrelated to MS.
A normal scan means lower MS risk.

steps.x: **D. Periventricular white matter lesions.** MRI in ON = look for MS plaques.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has painful blurred vision in her left eye for 5 days with red desaturation and a left RAPD. A medical student asks which approach is the gold standard for confirming optic neuritis. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the gold standard for diagnosis?
questions.e: Optic neuritis is a clinical diagnosis supported by MRI.

clues: red desaturation and a left RAPD
steps.x: Clinical picture plus **MRI**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical diagnosis plus MRI.

elim: Poor for the optic nerve and demyelination.
Can support MS but does not diagnose optic neuritis.
A specialist adjunct, not the gold standard.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis with MRI.** Gold standard = clinical + MRI.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman had possible optic neuritis 1 year ago. Her acuity and fundi are now normal, and her MRI is equivocal. She has a mild residual right RAPD and reduced red saturation. The neurologist wants a test showing delayed conduction along the optic nerve. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Nerve conduction studies of the legs
questions.e: Visual evoked potentials show slowed conduction from demyelination of the optic nerve, even after recovery.

clues: acuity and fundi are now normal
delayed conduction along the optic nerve
steps.x: Demyelination **slows conduction**. Which test times the signal?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Visual evoked potentials.

elim: Tests the retina, not the optic nerve.

steps.x: **E. Visual evoked potentials.** VEP = delayed conduction in the optic nerve.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman had left optic neuritis 9 months ago. Her left disc now looks pale. The ophthalmologist wants a quick non-invasive scan to measure thinning of the retinal nerve fibre layer. Her acuity is 6/9 left and 6/6 right. She has a mild left RAPD. Her MRI brain showed no lesions.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: OCT is a specialist test measuring retinal nerve fibre layer thinning after optic neuritis.

steps.x: **Optic atrophy** = nerve fibre loss. Measure the layer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: OCT.

elim: For seeing behind a cloudy media, not nerve fibre layers.

steps.x: **E. Optical coherence tomography.** Specialist tests: OCT and VEP.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has severe visual loss in both eyes that developed over 3 days. She also has numb legs and difficulty passing urine. Her MRI spine shows a cord lesion over 6 vertebral segments. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which blood test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Bilateral rapid optic neuritis with longitudinally extensive myelitis is NMO, confirmed by anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies.

clues: both eyes that developed over 3 days
steps.x: Bilateral ON + **long cord lesion** = NMO.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies.
**B. Anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies.** NMO = AQP4 antibodies.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman is diagnosed with left optic neuritis in eye casualty. She has painful blurred vision and a left RAPD. The ophthalmologist confirms there is no mimic on examination and arranges an MRI. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which specialist should also assess her?
questions.e: All suspected optic neuritis cases are referred to neurology, as it may be the first sign of MS.

steps.x: Optic neuritis may be the **first sign of MS**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neurology.

elim: Only if a vasculitis or connective tissue cause is suspected.

steps.x: **C. Neurology.** Every suspected case goes to neurology.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman is referred as possible right optic neuritis with eye pain and blurred vision for 2 days. Acuity is 6/18 in the right eye. Before treatment, the ophthalmologist examines her carefully to exclude a mimic, as a missed alternative diagnosis could cost her the eye. Five findings are considered.
questions.q: Which finding would most suggest an alternative diagnosis?
o: Red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil
questions.e: A red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma; mimics such as AACG, retinal detachment, uveitis and stroke must be excluded first.

clues: eye pain and blurred vision for 2 days
steps.x: Four of these are optic neuritis. Which is **not**?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Red eye with fixed mid-dilated pupil (AACG).
**E. Red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil.** Exclude mimics before treating: AACG, RD, uveitis, stroke.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with right optic neuritis and acuity of 6/60 has received 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone. Her eye pain has settled and her vision is starting to improve. She asks what happens next. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
questions.e: The standard acute treatment is IV methylprednisolone followed by a tapering course of oral prednisolone.

steps.x: IV methylprednisolone **then oral prednisolone**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral prednisolone taper.

elim: MS treatment is decided by neurology after MRI.
For severe steroid-unresponsive cases, especially NMO.
Standard treatment is followed by an oral taper.

steps.x: **C. Oral prednisolone taper.** IV methylpred, then oral pred taper.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman is referred from her GP with blurred vision in her left eye and an ache around the eye for 3 days. The GP thinks it is optic neuritis. Before anything else, the eye casualty doctor considers what must be done before starting steroids. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step?
o: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude mimics
Prescribe oral prednisolone and review in 6 weeks
questions.e: Before treating, confirm the diagnosis and exclude mimics such as acute angle-closure glaucoma, retinal detachment, uveitis or stroke.

clues: The GP thinks it is optic neuritis
steps.x: Diagnosis first, **then** steroids.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude mimics.

elim: Treat only once the diagnosis is confirmed.
Optic neuritis needs assessment and follow-up.

steps.x: **A. Confirm the diagnosis and exclude mimics.** Exclude mimics before treating.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman is recovering from left optic neuritis. Her MRI brain shows four ovoid periventricular lesions and one in the cervical cord. She has never had other neurological symptoms. Her acuity is now 6/9. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Neurology review to assess her multiple sclerosis risk
questions.e: If MRI shows demyelinating lesions, assess MS risk with neurology; optic neuritis may be the first sign of MS.

steps.x: Demyelinating lesions on MRI = **high MS risk**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neurology to assess MS risk.

elim: Lesions mean a high MS risk.
Far too late to act on high risk.
For severe refractory attacks, not recovery.

steps.x: **C. Neurology review to assess her multiple sclerosis risk.** MRI lesions: assess MS risk.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has mild right optic neuritis with acuity of 6/9. He is offered intravenous methylprednisolone but is worried about side effects and asks what would happen to his vision without it. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 120/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate advice?
o: He will become blind without steroids
Steroids are essential to lower his MS risk
Vision usually recovers, and steroids only speed recovery
Without steroids the other eye will be affected
questions.e: Steroids accelerate visual recovery by reducing inflammation and oedema but do not change long-term vision or MS risk, so declining is reasonable in mild cases.

clues: what would happen to his vision without it
steps.x: Steroids = **faster** recovery, **same** outcome.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Recovery is likely; steroids speed it up.

elim: Steroids do not change MS conversion risk.

steps.x: **D. Vision usually recovers, and steroids only speed recovery.** Steroids speed recovery, not the outcome.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man is about to start treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. He has no eye problems. His weight is 72 kg and renal function is normal.
questions.q: Which baseline test is most important before starting treatment because of the risk to the optic nerve?
questions.e: Ethambutol can cause optic neuritis, so baseline and ongoing visual acuity and colour vision monitoring are needed.

steps.x: **Ethambutol** = optic nerve toxicity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acuity and colour vision testing.
**E. Visual acuity and colour vision.** Ethambutol: check acuity and colour vision.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has recovered from right optic neuritis. Her MRI showed two white matter lesions and neurology have seen her once. She asks whether she needs to be seen again now that her vision is back to 6/6. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate plan?
o: Discharge to GP with no further follow-up
questions.e: Optic neuritis may be the first sign of MS, and recurrence can occur, so ongoing ophthalmology and neurology follow-up is needed.

steps.x: **First sign of MS** + recurrence risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ongoing joint follow-up.

elim: Does not prevent MS or recurrence.

steps.x: **D. Ongoing ophthalmology and neurology follow-up.** Follow up: ON may be the first sign of MS.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has left optic neuritis. Her MRI shows enhancement of the left optic nerve and periventricular white matter lesions. A medical student asks what is happening in the nerve. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the underlying pathological process?
o: Ischaemic infarction of the nerve head
questions.e: Optic neuritis is inflammatory demyelination of the optic nerve, most commonly a manifestation of MS.

clues: enhancement of the left optic nerve
steps.x: Enhancing nerve + MS-type lesions = **inflammatory demyelination**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inflammatory demyelination.

elim: Not the cause of typical optic neuritis.

steps.x: **C. Inflammatory demyelination.** ON = inflammatory demyelination, usually MS.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with right optic neuritis has acuity of 6/9 in the right eye but scores only 5 of 17 on Ishihara plates in that eye. The left eye scores 17 of 17. A student asks why colour is so affected when acuity is nearly normal.
questions.q: Which best explains this?
o: Colour vision is particularly sensitive to slowed optic nerve conduction
Cone cells in the retina are destroyed
The occipital colour area is damaged
questions.e: Demyelination slows or blocks conduction along the optic nerve, and colour vision is particularly sensitive to this, so colour falls before acuity.

steps.x: Near-normal acuity but **poor colour**: colour is most sensitive to **conduction block**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Colour is particularly sensitive to slowed conduction.

elim: This is an optic nerve, not a macular, problem.

steps.x: **A. Colour vision is particularly sensitive to slowed optic nerve conduction.** Demyelination: colour falls before acuity.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has left optic neuritis. The pain is dull at rest but sharp whenever she looks up or to either side. A student asks why moving the eye hurts when the problem is in the nerve. Her acuity is 6/18 left.
questions.q: Which best explains the pain?
o: Extraocular muscles stretch the inflamed nerve sheath
questions.e: The inflamed optic nerve is tethered to the extraocular muscles and orbital fascia, so eye movement stretches the inflamed sheath.

clues: sharp whenever she looks up or to either side
steps.x: Pain on **movement**: what attaches to the nerve sheath and moves?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Muscles stretching the inflamed sheath.

elim: Pressure is normal in optic neuritis.
Shooting facial pain, not linked to eye movement.

steps.x: **B. Extraocular muscles stretch the inflamed nerve sheath.** Pain on movement = stretch of inflamed nerve sheath.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has right optic neuritis. On the swinging light test, light in the left eye constricts both pupils. When the light swings to the right eye, both pupils dilate slightly. Both pupils are equal in size in normal light.
questions.q: Which part of the pupillary pathway is affected?
o: Afferent limb in the right optic nerve
Efferent limb in the right oculomotor nerve
Iris sphincter of the right eye
questions.e: A RAPD is due to reduced afferent conduction: light in the affected eye sends a weaker signal, so both pupils constrict less than with light in the healthy eye.

steps.x: Equal pupils, both react less when the right eye is lit: the **input** from the right is weak.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The afferent limb, right optic nerve.

elim: Damage would affect both pupils' constriction from both eyes.
Would give a fixed dilated right pupil and unequal pupils.

steps.x: **A. Afferent limb in the right optic nerve.** RAPD = afferent defect.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has bilateral optic neuritis and a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis. Her anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies are positive. Her MRI brain does not show typical MS lesions and CSF oligoclonal bands are absent. A student asks which cells the antibodies target.
questions.q: Which cell type is the main target?
questions.e: In NMO, anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies target astrocytes, giving a distinct and often more severe, bilateral and longitudinally extensive pattern than MS.

steps.x: Aquaporin-4 is a water channel on **astrocyte** foot processes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Astrocytes.

elim: Line the ventricles; not the target.
Immune cells, not the antibody target.
The main myelin-forming cells injured in MS.

steps.x: **A. Astrocytes.** NMO: AQP4 on astrocytes.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with left optic neuritis received IV methylprednisolone and her vision recovered within 2 weeks. Her friend, who declined steroids for the same condition, recovered over 2 months. At 1 year both have 6/6 vision. Both had normal MRI scans.
questions.q: Which best explains the effect of the steroids?
o: They cured the underlying multiple sclerosis
They reduced inflammation and oedema, speeding recovery
They regenerated the optic nerve axons
questions.e: Steroids accelerate visual recovery by reducing inflammation and oedema, but do not change long-term vision or MS conversion risk.

steps.x: Faster, but the **same endpoint**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reduced inflammation and oedema speeds recovery.

elim: Steroids do not alter MS risk.

steps.x: **D. They reduced inflammation and oedema, speeding recovery.** Steroids: quicker, not better.
